recall.define: Without opening the glossary, define mutex, condition variable, spurious wakeup, publication (memory ordering) and false sharing in one sentence each, naming the normative source for each.
recall.distinguish: For each pair, state the distinction and give a one-line C example that has the first but not the second: data race versus race condition; lock-free (atomic property) versus lock-free (progress guarantee); fence versus barrier (thread); volatile versus atomic operation; sequenced before versus happens before.
recall.apply: A worker thread publishes a filled buffer through a pointer and the consumer polls the pointer with relaxed loads. Using the terms publication (memory ordering), release sequence and synchronizes with, explain what the consumer may observe, which memory orders repair it, and which term applies to the remaining timing hazard once the data race is gone.

entries.definition: A mutual-exclusion lock that at most one thread holds at a time; unlocking it synchronizes with the next lock, so the critical section's writes happen before the next holder's reads. Ownership belongs to the locking thread, which is what distinguishes it from a binary semaphore.

authority.locator: §30.1 Protecting Accesses to Shared Variables: Mutexes, pp. 631–635

distinguish_from.distinction: A semaphore counts permits and may be released by a thread that never acquired it; a mutex is owned and must be released by its holder.

idiom: hold the mutex while reading the two fields together
entries.misconception: A mutex protects data (it protects a critical section; the discipline of taking it on every access is what protects the data).

entries.definition: A waiting primitive, always paired with a mutex, that lets a thread sleep until another thread signals that a predicate over shared state may have changed; the predicate is rechecked in a loop because wakeups can be spurious or stale.

authority.locator: §30.2.2 Signaling and Waiting on Condition Variables, pp. 643–647
DESCRIPTION, opening wait/mutex and predicate requirements

entries.misconception: A condition variable stores the condition (it stores nothing; the predicate lives in shared state guarded by the mutex).

entries.definition: A return from a condition-variable wait that no signal caused, which POSIX permits for efficiency; correct code therefore re-evaluates its predicate after every wakeup rather than assuming the condition holds.

authority.locator: §30.2.3 Testing a Condition Variable’s Predicate, pp. 647–648

idiom: guard against spurious wakeups with a predicate loop

entries.definition: A counter with atomic wait (decrement or block when zero) and post (increment and wake) operations; it has no owner, so it can signal across contexts, including from an interrupt handler to a thread, where a mutex cannot be used.
idiom: post the semaphore from the handler, wait in the thread
entries.misconception: A semaphore initialized to one is a mutex.

entries.definition: A lock that admits any number of concurrent readers or exactly one writer; it pays off only when read sections are long and frequent, because the extra bookkeeping and writer starvation policy cost more than a plain mutex on short sections.
entries.misconception: Read-write locks are always faster than mutexes for read-heavy workloads.

entries.definition: Objects with thread storage duration, declared thread_local (C23) or _Thread_local (C11), of which each thread has its own instance created when the thread starts and destroyed when it ends; the ELF TLS segment is the toolchain mechanism that implements it.

authority.locator: §6.6 Thread-Local Storage — mechanism, __thread declarations and address lifetime

distinguish_from.distinction: The ELF PT_TLS segment and the thread pointer are how the loader and libc realize thread storage duration; the language concept is the storage duration.

entries.misconception: errno is a global variable (it has thread storage duration).

entries.definition: A fixed set of worker threads that take tasks from a bounded queue, bounding concurrency and thread-creation cost; its design questions are queue capacity, backpressure when full, shutdown ordering and which thread runs a task's completion.
entries.misconception: More threads in the pool always mean more throughput.

entries.definition: A producer/consumer channel with a fixed capacity that blocks or rejects producers when full and consumers when empty; capacity is the backpressure mechanism that keeps memory use and latency bounded under overload.
idiom: the bounded queue applies backpressure to the producer
entries.misconception: An unbounded queue is simpler and therefore safer (it converts overload into memory exhaustion).

entries.definition: A state in which each thread of a set waits for a resource held by another thread of the set, so none can proceed; it requires mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait, and a global lock order removes the last condition.

distinguish_from.distinction: In a livelock threads keep running and changing state but make no progress; in a deadlock they are blocked.

idiom: acquire locks in a fixed global order to prevent deadlock
entries.misconception: A single lock cannot deadlock (a thread relocking a non-recursive mutex it holds deadlocks with itself).

entries.definition: A failure of progress in which threads repeatedly react to one another (retrying, backing off, yielding) without any of them completing; lock-free retry loops and overly polite collision avoidance both produce it.

The indefinite postponement of one thread while others keep making progress, caused by unfair scheduling, lock hand-off policy or priorities; fairness is the property that bounds how long any thread can be bypassed.
entries.misconception: A lock-free algorithm guarantees that every thread eventually completes (that is wait-freedom).

entries.definition: The situation in which a high-priority thread waits for a lock held by a low-priority thread that a medium-priority thread keeps preempting, so the effective priority order is inverted; priority inheritance or ceiling protocols bound it.
idiom: use a priority-inheritance mutex on the real-time path
entries.misconception: Priority inversion only matters on real-time operating systems.

entries.definition: A performance defect in which independent variables used by different cores share a cache line, so each write invalidates the other core's copy; correct, race-free code can still be slowed by orders of magnitude until the variables are padded to separate lines.
idiom: pad the per-thread counters to a cache line
entries.misconception: False sharing is a correctness bug.

entries.definition: The unit of transfer and coherence between a cache and memory, typically 64 bytes on x86-64 and 32 bytes on Cortex-M7; alignment of hot data to lines and ownership of whole lines by DMA buffers are decided at this granularity.
entries.misconception: Cache coherence means memory operations are ordered (coherence is per location; ordering across locations is the memory model's job).

entries.definition: The atomic read-modify-write that stores a new value only if the object still holds the expected value, returning whether it did and updating the expected value otherwise; the weak form may fail spuriously and belongs in loops, the strong form does not.
idiom: loop on compare_exchange_weak until the update lands
entries.misconception: A successful compare-and-exchange proves nothing changed in between (the ABA problem).

entries.definition: Making data written by one thread visible to another by a release operation on a flag or pointer that the reader acquires: the writes before the release happen before everything after the matching acquire. Without the release/acquire pair the reader may see the pointer but stale contents.

distinguish_from.distinction: Publication across threads concerns visibility in memory; a durable commit concerns survival of data across a crash. The curriculum uses 'publish' for the first and 'commit' for the second.

idiom: publish the node with a release store
entries.misconception: Once the pointer is visible, the object it points to is visible too (only with release/acquire ordering).

entries.definition: The release operation on an atomic object together with the subsequent read-modify-write operations on it; an acquire that reads any value written by the sequence synchronizes with the head release, which is what makes reference counting with fetch_add correct.
entries.misconception: An intervening relaxed store by another thread keeps the release sequence alive (only read-modify-writes extend it).

entries.definition: A construct such as an asm volatile statement with a memory clobber that forbids the compiler from moving memory accesses across it, without emitting any instruction; it constrains code generation only and gives no ordering guarantee to other processors or devices.

distinguish_from.distinction: A fence is the language-level ordering operation that the implementation maps to a hardware barrier when needed; a compiler barrier alone is enough only for single-processor interrupt code.

entries.misconception: A compiler barrier orders accesses as seen by another core.

entries.definition: A processor instruction (DMB, DSB, ISB on Arm; MFENCE on x86-64) that constrains the order in which the processor's memory accesses become visible or complete; the implementation's tool for realizing fences and release/acquire semantics.
entries.misconception: Inserting DMB everywhere makes code correct (barriers order; they do not make non-atomic accesses atomic).
